title: Kubernetes
objectives: Understand Kubernetes via a real-life analogy
Model Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMaps, Secrets
Deploy a backend + database + expose it

sections.markdown:
**Think of Kubernetes as a datacenter operating system — scheduling processes across many machines.**

Docker gives you containers. Kubernetes (k8s) orchestrates thousands of them across a cluster of nodes:

- **Node** — one server (VM or bare metal).
- **Cluster** — many nodes managed as one.
- **Pod** — smallest deployable unit; one or more tightly-coupled containers sharing network + storage.
- **Deployment** — declares 'I want N replicas of pod X'; handles rolling updates + rollbacks.
- **Service** — stable network endpoint for a set of pods (load-balances).
- **Ingress** — HTTP router (host + path) to services; terminates TLS.
- **ConfigMap / Secret** — config + secrets injected into pods.
- **PersistentVolume / Claim** — durable storage.

**Declarative:** you describe DESIRED state in YAML; k8s reconciles ACTUAL to DESIRED. Node dies? Pods rescheduled. Traffic spikes? HorizontalPodAutoscaler adds replicas. Deploy new version? Rolling update with health checks.

**Why every backend beyond hobby scale ends up here:** manual server management doesn't scale; ad-hoc orchestration (bash + cron) breaks; k8s is the industry standard for containerized workloads. GKE / EKS / AKS make it operable without full-time SREs at small scale.

**Flutter connection:** you don't deploy Flutter apps to k8s (they run on user devices). But your BACKEND — the auth service, the API, the EPCIS repo, the FCM sender — runs on k8s. Every serious Flutter product needs backend + backend needs k8s at some scale.

**Kubernetes (k8s)** is an open-source container orchestration system by Google (based on internal Borg). Cluster = **control plane** (API server, scheduler, controllers, etcd) + **worker nodes** (kubelet + container runtime). Objects (Pod, Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, Ingress, PersistentVolume) are declared via YAML and reconciled by controllers. Ecosystem tools: Helm (package manager), Kustomize (YAML overlays), operators (custom controllers).
## Core object cheat sheet

rows: One or more containers, shared network + storage
Declares desired # of replicas + rolling-update policy
Ordered pods with stable identity + persistent storage (databases)
One pod per node (log collector, metrics)
Sensitive data (base64-encoded, not encrypted by default)
Auto-scale based on CPU / memory / custom metrics

sections.markdown: ## Deploying a Node backend + Postgres

sections.code:
# ── deployment.yaml ──
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: api}
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: {maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0}
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: api}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: registry.example.com/api:1.2.3   # NEVER 'latest' in prod
        ports: [{containerPort: 3000}]
        env:
        - {name: NODE_ENV, value: production}
        - name: DATABASE_URL
          valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: db-creds, key: url}}
        resources:
          requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi}
          limits:   {cpu: 500m, memory: 256Mi}
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /health, port: 3000}
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /ready, port: 3000}
---
# ── service.yaml ──
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: api}
spec:
  selector: {app: api}
  ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 3000}]
---
# ── ingress.yaml ──
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: api
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  tls: [{hosts: [api.example.com], secretName: api-tls}]
  rules:
  - host: api.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - {path: /, pathType: Prefix, backend: {service: {name: api, port: {number: 80}}}}
---
# ── secret.yaml (in real life: created via kubectl, sealed-secrets, or external-secrets) ──
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata: {name: db-creds}
type: Opaque
stringData:
  url: postgres://user:pass@db-postgresql:5432/app

sections.markdown: ## HPA + rolling update commands

sections.code:
# Apply manifests
kubectl apply -f k8s/

# Scale + autoscale
kubectl scale deploy/api --replicas=5
kubectl autoscale deploy/api --min=3 --max=20 --cpu-percent=70

# Rolling update
kubectl set image deploy/api api=registry.example.com/api:1.2.4
kubectl rollout status deploy/api
kubectl rollout undo deploy/api    # rollback

# Debug
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl describe pod <name>
kubectl logs -f <pod> -c api
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh
kubectl top pods                    # CPU/memory

# Port-forward for local debugging
kubectl port-forward svc/api 3000:80

# Delete
kubectl delete -f k8s/

sections.markdown: ## Common mistakes
**Mistake 1: `latest` tag in prod.** Rollback impossible; deployment picks up random image. Always version-tag.
**Mistake 2: No resource requests/limits.** Pods eat everything; noisy-neighbor kills; OOM cascades. Always set.
**Mistake 3: No liveness/readiness probes.** Bad pods stay in rotation; users hit errors. Health checks matter.
**Mistake 4: Storing state in Deployment.** Restart = data gone. Use StatefulSet + PVC for databases.
**Mistake 5: Secrets as base64 in Git.** k8s Secret is base64 (not encrypted); commit = leak. Use sealed-secrets or external-secrets-operator.
**Mistake 6: RBAC too permissive.** Give service accounts minimum roles; audit.
**Mistake 7: No NetworkPolicy.** Any pod can talk to any pod; lateral movement paradise. Restrict.
**Mistake 8: Manual kubectl apply in prod.** Not versioned + not audited. Use GitOps (Argo CD / Flux).
## Best practices
**1. Version-tag images** — SHA or semver.
**2. Resource requests + limits** on every container.
**3. Liveness + readiness probes** on HTTP services.
**4. StatefulSets for stateful workloads.**
**5. sealed-secrets / external-secrets for secrets.**
**6. Least-privilege RBAC.**
**7. NetworkPolicy + PodSecurity.**
**8. GitOps (Argo CD / Flux)** — declarative infra + audit trail.
## Practice programs
**Practice 1 (Easy)** — Deploy an nginx pod + expose via NodePort in `minikube`/`kind`.
**Practice 2 (Medium)** — Deployment + Service + Ingress + TLS via cert-manager.
**Practice 3 (Medium)** — ConfigMap + Secret injected into a pod.
**Practice 4 (Hard)** — StatefulSet with Postgres + PVC + backup CronJob.
**Practice 5 (Hard)** — HPA + load-test; observe scale-up + scale-down.
**Practice 6 (Expert)** — GitOps: Argo CD syncing from a Git repo; blue-green deploy.
## Interview Q&A

**Q1: What is a Pod + why not deploy containers directly?**

**A:** A **Pod** is Kubernetes' smallest deployable unit: one or more tightly-coupled containers that share **network** (same IP, `localhost` communication) + **storage** (shared volumes) + **lifecycle**. Why not just 'a container' as the unit? Because **sidecars** are useful: a main app container + a log-shipping sidecar + an Istio-proxy sidecar all running together. **All containers in a pod share the fate** — pod dies = all containers stop. **In practice** — most pods have ONE main container; multi-container pods are for sidecars. **Direct pod deployment is rare** — you deploy a **Deployment** (or StatefulSet), which manages a set of pods with replication + rolling updates. Directly running a pod = no self-healing (pod dies, nothing replaces it). Interviewer signal: knowing pod vs Deployment distinction.

**Q2: Walk through a rolling update.**

**A:** **Trigger:** `kubectl set image deploy/api api=new:1.2.4` OR update manifest + `kubectl apply`. **Deployment controller sees new spec + creates a new ReplicaSet** for the new image; scales it up gradually. `maxSurge` = extra pods above desired (usually 25% or 1); `maxUnavailable` = pods you can lose (usually 0). **Sequence:** new pod created + waits for readiness probe green → OLD pod deleted → next new pod → next old pod deleted → until fully rolled. **If new pod's readiness fails**, the rollout PAUSES; no more old pods removed. **Rollback:** `kubectl rollout undo deploy/api` — swaps back to prior ReplicaSet. **Advanced strategies:** Blue-Green (parallel deploy + traffic switch); Canary (5% new + 95% old, gradual shift via Argo Rollouts or Flagger). **Health checks matter enormously** — bad readiness probe = broken pods stay in rotation. Interviewer bonus: strategies + rollback.

**Q3: What is a Service + when to use each type?**

**A:** A **Service** provides a stable IP + DNS name for a set of pods (which come + go). Types: **(1) ClusterIP** (default) — internal IP; only reachable inside the cluster. Perfect for inter-service communication. **(2) NodePort** — opens the same port on every node; external traffic can hit any node's IP:port. Basic external access; not recommended in prod. **(3) LoadBalancer** — cloud provider provisions an external LB (AWS ELB, GCP LB); external traffic → LB → pods. Best for external HTTP if you don't need Ingress. **(4) ExternalName** — DNS alias to an external service. **Ingress** — separate object above Services for HTTP routing (host + path) + TLS termination. **Practical prod pattern:** ClusterIP Services for internal + one Ingress + one LoadBalancer for the Ingress controller. **Interviewer signal:** knowing when each fits + not confusing Service with Ingress.

**Q4: How are secrets handled + what's the recommended pattern?**

**A:** k8s **Secret** object stores sensitive data — BUT it's **base64-encoded, NOT encrypted** at rest by default. `kubectl get secret X -o yaml` reveals values instantly. **Attack surface:** anyone with cluster read access + committed-to-git manifests. **Best practice:** **(1) Encryption at rest** — configure kube-apiserver `EncryptionConfiguration` (AES-256). **(2) Sealed Secrets (Bitnami)** — encrypted secrets in git; controller decrypts in-cluster. **(3) External Secrets Operator** — pulls from AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager / Vault; syncs to k8s Secret. **(4) Vault agent injector** — sidecar mounts secrets at runtime. **(5) SPIFFE/SPIRE** — workload identity → cloud IAM without static secrets. **Rotation:** all these support rotation. **Interviewer signal:** naming multiple mature options + knowing base64 ≠ encryption.

**Q5: What are Requests vs Limits + why do they matter?**

**A:** **Requests** = minimum resources the scheduler reserves for the pod on a node. Used for scheduling decisions (fit-first). **Limits** = maximum resources the pod can use before enforcement (CPU throttled; memory → OOMKill). **CPU:** millicores; `100m` = 0.1 core. **Memory:** bytes; `128Mi` = 128 mebibytes. **QoS classes:** (1) **Guaranteed** — requests == limits; highest priority; last evicted under pressure. (2) **Burstable** — requests < limits; middle. (3) **BestEffort** — no requests/limits; first evicted. **Anti-patterns:** (a) no requests → pods pile onto one node → node crash. (b) no limits → one bad pod eats all memory → OOM cascade. (c) requests too high → wasted capacity + fewer pods per node. **Right-sizing:** measure actual usage + tune; Vertical Pod Autoscaler can automate. **Interviewer bonus:** knowing QoS classes.

**Q6: How would you architect a Flutter product's backend on Kubernetes?**

**A:** **(1) Cluster:** GKE / EKS / AKS — managed control plane; ~3-node worker pool minimum. **(2) Namespaces:** `dev`, `staging`, `prod` — isolation + quotas. **(3) Backend Deployments** — API + auth + push-sender + EPCIS repo, each 3+ replicas. **(4) StatefulSet + PVC** for Postgres (or cloud-managed RDS/Cloud SQL — usually preferred). **(5) Redis + Kafka** — managed services (Elasticache, Confluent Cloud) or in-cluster StatefulSets. **(6) Ingress + cert-manager** for HTTPS. **(7) HorizontalPodAutoscaler** — 3 min, 20 max, target 70% CPU. **(8) Prometheus + Grafana + Loki** for metrics + logs. **(9) External Secrets Operator** → GCP Secret Manager. **(10) GitOps via Argo CD** — cluster reconciles from git. **(11) CI (GitHub Actions) builds + pushes images + updates manifest + Argo syncs.** **(12) Distroless images + non-root + NetworkPolicy + PodSecurity.** **(13) Sentry + Crashlytics** for error tracking. **(14) OTel** for tracing. **(15) Cost monitoring** — kubecost / GCP Recommender. **Interviewer signal:** end-to-end architecture including security + observability + GitOps.

## Real-world usage

- **Every scale-up backend** for Flutter products.
- **Multi-tenant SaaS** — namespaces per tenant OR pod-per-tenant depending on isolation.
- **Microservices** — dozens of small services.
- **Batch + streaming** — Jobs + CronJobs + Kafka.
- **NOT ideal for** — Flutter apps themselves (they run on user devices).

## Advanced notes

- **Helm** — package manager; charts template YAML.
- **Kustomize** — overlays without templating (built into `kubectl`).
- **Argo CD / Flux** — GitOps controllers.
- **Argo Rollouts / Flagger** — canary + blue-green.
- **Istio / Linkerd** — service mesh (mTLS + traffic policy + tracing).
- **Cilium** — CNI + eBPF-based observability.
- **cert-manager** — automated TLS via Let's Encrypt.
- **Sealed Secrets / External Secrets** — secret management.
- **OPA / Kyverno** — policy engines.
- **Cluster autoscaler** — nodes scale up/down.
- **VPA (Vertical Pod Autoscaler)** — right-size requests.
- **KEDA** — event-driven autoscaling (queue depth, etc.).
- **Longhorn / Rook** — cloud-native storage.
- **etcd** — control plane database; backup regularly.
- **kube-bench** — CIS benchmark.
- **Falco** — runtime security.
- **Chaos Mesh** — chaos engineering.
- **Backstage** — dev portal on top of k8s.
- **Karpenter** — smarter node provisioning (AWS).
